paragraphs.text: A loose [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, the undarkened branch of the family, never given the quick fermentation that makes shou. It begins as leaf from the province’s large-leaf tea trees, picked and withered, then fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making), rolled, and dried in the sun over a couple of days. What comes out is [maocha](sheng:processing), the rough tea, and here it has been left loose instead of steamed and pressed into a cake.

The wok heat stops most of the leaf’s own enzymes but not all, and because the leaf is never hot-air dried afterwards, the activity that survives lets it keep [changing through storage](sheng:aging) for years. Where and how it is kept becomes part of its history.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.
